source: Gugerty & Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Two experiments (LOGO in Exp 1, Pascal in Exp 2) on programs given to the subject and run on a microcomputer. Experts debugged faster and more accurately, largely because they made good hypotheses after studying the code less. Novices often added bugs while hunting the original one.
numbers: Abstract only (ACM and Academia full text blocked with 403). No sample sizes or effect sizes could be read.
quote: Experts debugged more quickly and accurately, largely because they generated high quality hypotheses on the basis of less study of the code
limits: Simple programs only. Authors put the expert edge mainly on program comprehension.
agent_relevance: Comprehension before edit. Every edit is a chance to add a bug, so keep best-so-far and cap edits per round.

source: Gugerty & Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Authors' conclusion: for these simple programs, experts' superior debugging seemed due primarily to superior ability to comprehend the program.
numbers: Abstract-level claim; no numbers read.
quote: At least for these simple programs, experts superior debugging performance seemed to be due primarily to their superior ability to comprehend the program
limits: Qualified by the authors themselves: simple programs.
agent_relevance: The gap is in understanding, not in editing skill. Spend early tokens on understanding (S1, S2) and gate edits on a stated hypothesis.

source: Kinnunen (2007) MSc thesis on debugging with Jeliot (secondary account of G&O)
finding: A thesis summary of G&O: participants read the description and code, form a hypothesis, test it by editing, running or checking the spec, and return to reading if no error is found. Novices and experts did not act differently in this loop, but novices needed more time, seldom found the bug at first try, and added new bugs.
numbers: No numbers. Second-hand.
limits: Second-hand citation; treat as [S].
agent_relevance: The loop is the same for strong and weak solvers. Hypothesis quality is what differs, so gate on it, not on step order.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs
finding: Verbal-protocol study of 16 practising programmers (8 expert, 8 novice), classed by chunking ability. Chunking class explained 73.7% of variance in debug time; manager rating only 36.1%.
numbers: Mean debug time: experts 15 min 40 s, novices 28 min 3 s. By manager rating: 20 min 24 s versus 23 min 19 s. N=16, one program per subject, two bug levels.
limits: Small N, one organisation, exploratory.
agent_relevance: Skill is comprehension (chunking), not rank or years. Judge by what the solver shows, not by a label.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs
finding: Closest human replication of 'novices add bugs'. All 5 programmers who made incorrect repairs were novices on the chunking classification. Novices made significantly more errors (P=0.005, R2=0.50) and needed more episodes (P=0.003, R2=0.57).
numbers: 8 mistakes in total, 6 on the low-level bug. Manager rating classed only 4 of the 5 error-makers as novices.
limits: Different task, language and sample from G&O, which strengthens agreement. Small N; a mistake counted when the experimenter told the subject the repair was wrong.
agent_relevance: Wrong repairs are the novice signature. Count regressions per round in code and stop the round at the first one.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs
finding: Mechanism: experts built a causal model of the whole system early ('system thinking') and searched breadth-first. Novices did not. Time per episode did not differ; novices needed more episodes and more major phases.
numbers: Episodes: novice > expert, P=0.003. Time per episode: no difference by group.
limits: Exploratory protocol analysis, N=16.
agent_relevance: A global model first. Our S2 REPRESENT step should come before any edit.

source: Ko & Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies
finding: 75 participants in an unfamiliar statistical language, 20-minute debug task. Three comprehension strategies appeared. No strategy gave best debugging. Success followed domain knowledge of the specific bug and attitude toward computers.
numbers: Bugs fixed (of 4): depth-first cluster 1.00 (SD 0.97), clusters 2 and 3: 1.65 (0.98) and 2.00 (1.07). Programming experience means 2.52, 1.20, 3.59.
quote: no particular strategy resulted in the best debugging performance
limits: Boundary: unfamiliar system weakens the expert edge. Undergraduate sample, one task.
agent_relevance: Expert edge depends on domain knowledge. On problem classes the agent knows little, hypothesis quality falls, so lean on checks and exploration.

source: Davies (2000) Expertise and the comprehension of object-oriented programs
finding: 32 participants (16 novice, 16 expert) saw object-oriented programs briefly. Experts pulled out information quickly and accurately. As presentation length grew, novices and experts did not differ in comprehension categories.
numbers: N=32, mixed design: expertise between subjects, presentation time within.
quote: as presentation length increases, there is no difference between novices and experts
limits: Comprehension, not debugging. Object-oriented code only.
agent_relevance: Supports 'less reading' as speed of extraction. With a generous budget a weaker reader can close the gap, so budget reading by difficulty (G12).

source: Crossref metadata for Katz & Anderson 1987 (HCI 3(4) 351-399)
finding: Citation correction. HCI 3(4) 351-399 (1987) is Katz & Anderson, 'Debugging: an analysis of bug-location strategies'. It is not a long version of G&O, as an earlier search snippet implied.
numbers: Crossref shows 143 citations for Katz & Anderson. Fitzgerald et al. 2008 (145) and McCauley et al. 2008 (227) exist but no text was read.
limits: Metadata only. Katz & Anderson is the likeliest source of a quantitative bug-location replication and is still unread.
agent_relevance: Do not cite a 1987 journal version of G&O. Read Katz & Anderson and McCauley 2008 next.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Self-repair (generate, explain, repair) on HumanEval and APPS with Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. When repair cost is counted, gains are modest, vary by subset, and are sometimes absent.
numbers: Normalised pass rate versus resampling at equal budget, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 cells, about 0.92 to 1.11. Below 1 means repair loses to plain resampling; small budgets are worst.
limits: 2023 models, three families.
agent_relevance: LLM analogue of risky edits: at equal tokens fresh samples often beat repair. Supports G7 and a cap on repair rounds.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Holding repairs per program fixed, more initial programs always helped. Holding initial programs fixed, more repairs per program gave marginal or negative returns. Diversity of first drafts mattered more than diversity of repairs.
numbers: Heat maps Fig. 3-4; cells over 50 samples not run.
limits: Same models and benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Keep best-so-far across several drafts and repair few. Matches 'limit edits per round'.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Feedback quality is the bottleneck, as hypothesis quality is for human novices. Expert human feedback raised GPT-4 repair success from 33.30% to 52.60%.
numbers: Table 1 (GPT-4 vs human feedback): introductory 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67. 16 participants, 40 failing programs, 2 feedbacks each, 25 repairs per feedback. Ratio 1.58x.
limits: Small paid human study; cost of human time not charged.
agent_relevance: G&O in LLM form: repair works when the hypothesis about the fault is good. Locate faults by code and real output (G2).

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Competing explanation tested: weak repair is due to weak feedback on its own code, not weak rewriting. Swapping in a stronger feedback model let Code Llama and GPT-3.5 beat both baseline and self-repair on APPS.
numbers: Experiment 4.2; Code Llama with GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 feedback; GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 feedback.
limits: Feedback model cost is an extra expense not equalised in every plot.
agent_relevance: Cross-model feedback also breaks same-model error correlation (G4); worth a test.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Self-Debugging: run the code, explain it line by line (rubber duck), read feedback, repair. Spider +2 to 3 points, hardest SQL +9, TransCoder and MBPP up to +12 with unit tests.
numbers: Explanation alone without debugging: +2 to 3 on code translation. MBPP gain about 8 for one model with unit tests.
limits: Early-2023 models (Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, StarCoder).
agent_relevance: Execution feedback pays; explanation alone is small but cheap comprehension before editing.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Self-debugging also improved sample efficiency: fewer initial samples were needed for the same accuracy, by reusing failed predictions.
numbers: Claim in abstract and introduction.
limits: Needs an executor.
agent_relevance: Use failed attempts as information instead of discarding them.

source: Adnan & Kuhn (2025) The Debugging Decay Index
finding: Debugging effectiveness decays exponentially over attempts. Most models lose 60-80% of their debugging effectiveness within 2-3 attempts (18 models, HumanEval). A fresh start (clear history) at computed points helps at the same attempt budget.
numbers: phi4:14b 83.5 first pass to 93.3 final; phi4-reasoning 59.1 to 81.1 (+21.95 vs +9.75). gpt-3.5-turbo reaches the 80% decay threshold by attempt 2-3. Claude-3.7-Sonnet hit 100% in two attempts so no fit.
quote: most models lose 60-80% of their debugging capability within just 2-3 attempts
limits: Several fits poor (R2 under 0.7); preprint; HumanEval near ceiling for strong models; fresh-start tables only partly read.
agent_relevance: Cap repair rounds near 3, then restart from the problem statement and keep best-so-far (G6). Same budget.

source: Adnan & Kuhn (2025) The Debugging Decay Index
finding: Reasoning-tuned model sustained debugging better than its non-reasoning sibling: lower decay constant for phi4-reasoning than phi4.
numbers: Table says 0.60 vs 0.76; text says 0.591 vs 0.711. The paper is inconsistent.
limits: One model pair; internal inconsistency.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that reasoning models behave more like experts in sustained repair.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: BIG-Bench Mistake has 2186 chain-of-thought traces with the first mistake marked. LLMs find the mistake poorly. GPT-4 reaches only 52.87 overall with direct step-level prompting.
numbers: GPT-4 logical deduction 40.67 (direct step); GPT-3.5-Turbo 10.10 on one task. Traces sampled 85% incorrect, 15% correct.
quote: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
limits: Tasks are word sorting, object tracking, logic, arithmetic, Dyck; fairly synthetic.
agent_relevance: Forming the fault hypothesis is the novice-like step for LLMs. Let code find the location; do not ask the model to guess it (G2).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Given the true mistake location, redoing the step fixes many errors, but it also breaks some traces that were right. Word sorting: 11.11% of correct traces became wrong and 23.53% of wrong traces became right.
numbers: Tracking shuffled objects: base accuracy 50% gives 68.6%; base 99% gives 92.8%.
limits: Uses oracle locations; real locators are noisy.
agent_relevance: Same as novices adding bugs: editing what was right costs. Edit only after a check fails (G1).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: A modest trained locator is enough: on most tasks backtracking beats baseline once mistake-finding accuracy is about 60-70%.
numbers: Section 5.1, from text; approximate.
limits: Needs training data per task.
agent_relevance: A code-side or small-model fault locator at moderate accuracy is already useful.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without external feedback, self-correction on reasoning does not help and often hurts. GPT-3.5 on GSM8K keeps its answer 74.7% of the time, and among changes, correct-to-incorrect outnumber incorrect-to-correct.
numbers: GPT-3.5 standard prompting: GSM8K 75.9, CommonSenseQA 75.8, HotpotQA 26.0. Oracle-label rows give much higher numbers (looks good only because the label is leaked). Column alignment of Table 2 in the extracted text is uncertain.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction
limits: Two rounds only; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2. The model cannot tell right from wrong by itself.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Mechanism for self-edits making things worse: the model cannot judge its own reasoning. On CommonSenseQA the self-correct prompt pushes it to switch from correct to wrong because wrong options look relevant.
numbers: Higher change rate on CommonSenseQA than GSM8K; Llama-2 shows the same shift.
limits: Qualitative analysis in section 3.3.
agent_relevance: A scheduled 'review your answer' prompt acts like a blind novice edit. Do not use it (G1).

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes?
finding: Critical survey. (1) No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks unusually suited to it. (2) It works where reliable external feedback exists. (3) Large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Survey of many papers; no pooled effect size.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Many prior studies use unfair evaluations (oracle labels, weak baselines). Survey cut-off 2024.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2 and G3: revise from run outputs, tests and tools.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: Agentless, a fixed pipeline (localise, repair, validate) with no model-chosen actions, solved 32.00% (96 of 300) of SWE-bench Lite for $0.70 per issue, best among open-source agents then. Patches are filtered with regression tests plus generated reproduction tests.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite 300 issues. Authors also built Lite-S by removing issues with leaked patches or misleading text.
limits: Benchmark noise (leaked patches, weak issue text). 2024 model snapshot.
agent_relevance: Code fixes the order (localise first, edit once, validate) and beats free-roaming agents. Matches 'program decides transitions'.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Reflexion stores verbal reflections on failures for the next try. HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0 versus 80.1 for the GPT-4 baseline. Success depends on test quality; weak self-written tests can pass wrong code (false positives).
numbers: HumanEval (PY) 91.0 vs 80.1. Other rows in the extracted table are garbled, so not recorded.
limits: Self-generated tests are not independent of the generating model.
agent_relevance: Execution feedback on held-out tests (G3) is what makes reflection work.
